steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An analogue signal varies continuously in amplitude and time; a digital signal has discrete voltage levels.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Frequency response describes how a circuit's gain varies with frequency; it is typically plotted as a Bode diagram.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An RC low-pass filter allows frequencies below the cut-off to pass while attenuating higher frequencies.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An RC high-pass filter allows frequencies above the cut-off to pass while attenuating lower frequencies.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Calculate the cut-off frequency of an RC low-pass filter with R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. | Q: What is the roll-off rate of a first-order RC low-pass filter above the cut-off frequency? | Q: Explain the purpose of a voltage follower buffer in a filter circuit.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: f_c = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 1000 × 100 × 10⁻⁹) = 1/(6.283 × 10⁻⁴) = 1592 Hz ≈ 1.6 kHz. | −20 dB/decade, which is equivalent to −6 dB/octave. | A voltage follower provides high input impedance and low output impedance, preventing the filter from being loaded by the next stage.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always write the cut-off frequency formula f_c = 1/(2πRC) before substituting values. Convert all units to base SI (Ω, F, Hz) before calculating to avoid powers-of-ten errors. Remember: at the cut-off frequency, the output voltage is 0.707 × Vin (i.e. −3 dB), not zero. Distinguish between roll-off rates: first order = −20 dB/decade, second order = −40 dB/decade. When sketching Bode plots, mark the cut-off frequency clearly and show the −20 dB/decade slope.
